raw: CHAPTER III. The Night Shadows
en: [Chapter 3]

raw: A wonderful fact to reflect upon, that every human creature is constituted to be that profound secret and mystery to every other.
en: The Night Shadows It is a wonderful thing to think about.

raw: A solemn consideration, when I enter a great city by night, that every one of those darkly clustered houses encloses its own secret; that every room in every one of them encloses its own secret; that every beating heart in the hundreds of thousands of breasts there, is, in some of its imaginings, a secret to the heart nearest it!
en: It is a serious thought, when I enter a great city by night, that every one of those dark, clustered houses holds its own secret. Every room inside them holds its own secret, too. And every beating heart, among the hundreds of thousands of people there, holds secrets even from the person closest to them!

raw: Something of the awfulness, even of Death itself, is referable to this.
en: Every room in every house holds its own secret.

raw: No more can I turn the leaves of this dear book that I loved, and vainly hope in time to read it all.
en: Every beating heart among the hundreds of thousands of people there, in some of its deepest thoughts, is a secret even to the person standing closest to it.

raw: No more can I look into the depths of this unfathomable water, wherein, as momentary lights glanced into it, I have had glimpses of buried treasure and other things submerged.
en: I can no longer look into the depths of this deep, mysterious water, where, by brief flashes of light, I have caught glimpses of buried treasure and other hidden things.

raw: It was appointed that the book should shut with a spring, for ever and for ever, when I had read but a page.
en: The pages of a dear book snap shut before we ever finish reading it.

raw: It was appointed that the water should be locked in an eternal frost, when the light was playing on its surface, and I stood in ignorance on the shore.
en: The depths of a beautiful pool freeze over before we can see what lies at the bottom. My friend is dead.

raw: My friend is dead, my neighbour is dead, my love, the darling of my soul, is dead; it is the inexorable consolidation and perpetuation of the secret that was always in that individuality, and which I shall carry in mine to my life’s end.
en: My neighbor is dead. My love, the darling of my soul, is dead. The secret they carried is now sealed forever inside them. And I will carry my own secret until I die.

raw: In any of the burial-places of this city through which I pass, is there a sleeper more inscrutable than its busy inhabitants are, in their innermost personality, to me, or than I am to them?
en: Walking through any cemetery in this city, I have to wonder: are the people sleeping underground truly more mysterious than the people rushing past the gate above them?

raw: As to this, his natural and not to be alienated inheritance, the messenger on horseback had exactly the same possessions as the King, the first Minister of State, or the richest merchant in London.
en: When it came to this, this natural mystery that no one could take away, the messenger on horseback was equal to the King, the Prime Minister, or the richest merchant in London.

raw: So with the three passengers shut up in the narrow compass of one lumbering old mail coach; they were mysteries to one another, as complete as if each had been in his own coach and six, or his own coach and sixty, with the breadth of a county between him and the next.
en: The three passengers in that cramped old mail coach were no different. Each was a complete mystery to the others. They might as well each have been riding alone in a private carriage, with an entire county of open road between them.

raw: The messenger rode back at an easy trot, stopping pretty often at ale-houses by the way to drink, but evincing a tendency to keep his own counsel, and to keep his hat cocked over his eyes.
en: The messenger rode back at an easy trot, stopping pretty often at pubs along the way to drink, but showing a tendency to keep to himself and keep his hat pulled low over his eyes.

raw: He had eyes that assorted very well with that decoration, being of a surface black, with no depth in the colour or form, and much too near together--as if they were afraid of being found out in something, singly, if they kept too far apart.
en: He had eyes that went well with that look: they were flat black, with no depth in color or shape, and set much too close together, as if they were afraid of being caught doing something separately if they stood too far apart.

raw: They had a sinister expression, under an old cocked-hat like a three-cornered spittoon, and over a great muffler for the chin and throat, which descended nearly to the wearer’s knees.
en: They had a sinister look, hidden under an old cocked hat that looked like a three-cornered spittoon, and above a large scarf for his chin and throat that hung down almost to his knees.

raw: When he stopped for drink, he moved this muffler with his left hand, only while he poured his liquor in with his right; as soon as that was done, he muffled again.
en: When he stopped for a drink, he pulled this scarf away with his left hand only while pouring the alcohol in with his right; as soon as that was done, he wrapped himself back up.

raw: “No, Jerry, no!” said the messenger, harping on one theme as he rode. “It wouldn’t do for you, Jerry.
en: "No, Jerry, no!" said the messenger, repeating the same idea as he rode. "It wouldn't work out for you, Jerry.

raw: Jerry, you honest tradesman, it wouldn’t suit _your_ line of business!
en: Jerry, you honest tradesman, it wouldn't suit your line of work!

raw: Recalled--!
en: Recalled, !

raw: Bust me if I don’t think he’d been a drinking!”
en: Blow me if I don't think he's been drinking!"

raw: His message perplexed his mind to that degree that he was fain, several times, to take off his hat to scratch his head.
en: His message confused him so much that he kept having to take off his hat to scratch his head.

raw: Except on the crown, which was raggedly bald, he had stiff, black hair, standing jaggedly all over it, and growing down hill almost to his broad, blunt nose.
en: The top of his head was patchily bald. The rest of his hair was stiff, black, and jagged. It grew forward almost to his broad, flat nose.

raw: It was so like Smith’s work, so much more like the top of a strongly spiked wall than a head of hair, that the best of players at leap-frog might have declined him, as the most dangerous man in the world to go over.
en: It looked less like hair and more like the spikes on top of a stone wall. Even the best leapfrog player in the world would have thought twice before jumping over him.

raw: While he trotted back with the message he was to deliver to the night watchman in his box at the door of Tellson’s Bank, by Temple Bar, who was to deliver it to greater authorities within, the shadows of the night took such shapes to him as arose out of the message, and took such shapes to the mare as arose out of _her_ private topics of uneasiness.
en: As he trotted back to deliver his message, the night shadows played tricks on his mind. He was heading for the night watchman's booth at the door of Tellson's Bank, near Temple Bar. The watchman would pass the message on to the senior officials inside. As Jerry rode, the word "recalled" haunted him. Strange shapes formed in the dark.

raw: They seemed to be numerous, for she shied at every shadow on the road.
en: Even his mare seemed nervous, she shied away from every shadow on the road, as if the night were full of things only she could see.

raw: What time, the mail-coach lumbered, jolted, rattled, and bumped upon its tedious way, with its three fellow-inscrutables inside.
en: Meanwhile, the mail coach rumbled, jolted, rattled, and bumped along its exhausting path, with its three mysterious passengers inside.

raw: To whom, likewise, the shadows of the night revealed themselves, in the forms their dozing eyes and wandering thoughts suggested.
en: To them, too, the night shadows showed themselves in whatever shapes their sleepy eyes and wandering thoughts suggested.

raw: Tellson’s Bank had a run upon it in the mail.
en: Tellson's Bank was never far from the banker's thoughts.

raw: As the bank passenger--with an arm drawn through the leathern strap, which did what lay in it to keep him from pounding against the next passenger, and driving him into his corner, whenever the coach got a special jolt--nodded in his place, with half-shut eyes, the little coach-windows, and the coach-lamp dimly gleaming through them, and the bulky bundle of opposite passenger, became the bank, and did a great stroke of business.
en: He dozed in his seat, his arm hooked through the leather strap overhead to stop himself from slamming into the next passenger every time the coach jolted badly. The dim coach windows, the faint glow of the lamp, and the dark silhouette of the passenger across from him all slowly transformed in his half-sleeping mind into the familiar rooms of the bank.

raw: The rattle of the harness was the chink of money, and more drafts were honoured in five minutes than even Tellson’s, with all its foreign and home connection, ever paid in thrice the time.
en: The rattling of the harness sounded like the clinking of coins. In his mind, more bank drafts were cashed in five minutes than even Tellson's bank, with all its local and foreign connections, had ever paid out in three times as long.

raw: Then the strong-rooms underground, at Tellson’s, with such of their valuable stores and secrets as were known to the passenger (and it was not a little that he knew about them), opened before him, and he went in among them with the great keys and the feebly-burning candle, and found them safe, and strong, and sound, and still, just as he had last seen them.
en: More transactions were processed in five minutes of dreaming than Tellson's had managed in three times that duration in real life. Then the underground vaults opened in his mind. He walked through them with a large ring of keys and a dimly burning candle. He found everything exactly as he had left it: safe, secure, and perfectly quiet.

raw: But, though the bank was almost always with him, and though the coach (in a confused way, like the presence of pain under an opiate) was always with him, there was another current of impression that never ceased to run, all through the night.
en: But, even though he was constantly thinking about the bank, and even though he was always vaguely aware of the coach (like a dull pain felt through medication), there was another steady stream of thought that never stopped running through his mind all night.

raw: He was on his way to dig some one out of a grave.
en: He was on his way to dig someone out of a grave.

raw: Now, which of the multitude of faces that showed themselves before him was the true face of the buried person, the shadows of the night did not indicate; but they were all the faces of a man of five-and-forty by years, and they differed principally in the passions they expressed, and in the ghastliness of their worn and wasted state.
en: The night shadows refused to show him which face was the true face of that buried person. But every face that appeared was the face of a man around forty-five years old. All the faces were different in expression: some proud, some scornful, some defiant, some broken.

raw: Pride, contempt, defiance, stubbornness, submission, lamentation, succeeded one another; so did varieties of sunken cheek, cadaverous colour, emaciated hands and figures.
en: But all of them had sunken cheeks, deathly pale skin, and thin, skeletal hands.

raw: But the face was in the main one face, and every head was prematurely white.
en: And every single one of them had hair gone prematurely white.

raw: A hundred times the dozing passenger inquired of this spectre:
en: A hundred times that night, the dozing passenger asked the ghost the same question:

raw: “Buried how long?”
en: "Buried how long?"

raw: The answer was always the same: “Almost eighteen years.”
en: The answer was always the same: "Almost eighteen years."

raw: “You had abandoned all hope of being dug out?”
en: "You had given up all hope of being dug out?"

raw: “Long ago.”
en: "Long ago."

raw: “You know that you are recalled to life?”
en: "You know that you are brought back to life?"

raw: “They tell me so.”
en: "They tell me so."

raw: “I hope you care to live?”
en: "I hope you care to live?"

raw: “I can’t say.”
en: "I can't say."

raw: “Shall I show her to you?
en: "Shall I show her to you?

raw: Will you come and see her?”
en: Will you come and see her?"

raw: The answers to this question were various and contradictory.
en: The answers to this question were different and contradictory.

raw: Sometimes the broken reply was, “Wait!
en: Sometimes the shaky reply was, "Wait!

raw: It would kill me if I saw her too soon.”  Sometimes, it was given in a tender rain of tears, and then it was, “Take me to her.” Sometimes it was staring and bewildered, and then it was, “I don’t know her.
en: It would kill me if I saw her too soon." Sometimes it was spoken through a gentle flow of tears: "Take me to her." Sometimes it was wide-eyed and confused: "I don't know her.

raw: I don’t understand.”
en: I don't understand."

raw: After such imaginary discourse, the passenger in his fancy would dig, and dig, dig--now with a spade, now with a great key, now with his hands--to dig this wretched creature out.
en: After these imagined conversations, the passenger's dream-self would dig. And dig. And dig. Sometimes with a shovel, sometimes with a large key, sometimes with bare hands. The goal was always to pull this miserable creature out of the ground.

raw: Got out at last, with earth hanging about his face and hair, he would suddenly fan away to dust.
en: And when he finally did, when the man emerged, covered in dirt, the figure would suddenly crumble into dust.

raw: The passenger would then start to himself, and lower the window, to get the reality of mist and rain on his cheek.
en: The passenger would then jolt awake. He would roll down the window and press his cheek against the cold, wet mist to feel something real.

raw: Yet even when his eyes were opened on the mist and rain, on the moving patch of light from the lamps, and the hedge at the roadside retreating by jerks, the night shadows outside the coach would fall into the train of the night shadows within.
en: But even with his eyes open, seeing the mist, the moving patch of coach-lamp light, the roadside hedges jerking past, the night shadows outside the coach would always bleed back into the night shadows in his mind.

raw: The real Banking-house by Temple Bar, the real business of the past day, the real strong rooms, the real express sent after him, and the real message returned, would all be there.
en: The real bank near Temple Bar. The real business from yesterday. The real vaults. The real messenger. The real reply.

raw: Out of the midst of them, the ghostly face would rise, and he would accost it again.
en: All of it was there. And right in the middle of it all, the ghostly face would rise again. And he would ask the same question.

raw: “Buried how long?”
en: "Buried how long?"

raw: “Almost eighteen years.”
en: "Almost eighteen years."

raw: “I hope you care to live?”
en: "I hope you care to live?"

raw: “I can’t say.”
en: "I can't say."

raw: Dig--dig--dig--until an impatient movement from one of the two passengers would admonish him to pull up the window, draw his arm securely through the leathern strap, and speculate upon the two slumbering forms, until his mind lost its hold of them, and they again slid away into the bank and the grave.
en: Dig. Dig. Dig. Until one of the other passengers shifted restlessly, snapping him back to reality. He would roll the window back up. He would hook his arm through the strap again. He would try to focus on the two sleeping figures nearby. But soon his mind would drift away. Back to the bank. Back to the grave.

raw: “Buried how long?”
en: "Buried how long?"

raw: “Almost eighteen years.”
en: "Almost eighteen years."

raw: “You had abandoned all hope of being dug out?”
en: "You had given up all hope of being dug out?"

raw: “Long ago.”
en: "Long ago."

raw: The words were still in his hearing as just spoken--distinctly in his hearing as ever spoken words had been in his life--when the weary passenger started to the consciousness of daylight, and found that the shadows of the night were gone.
en: The words were still ringing in his ears when he woke up. They were as clear as any words he had ever heard spoken aloud. He startled awake to the morning light. The night shadows were gone.

raw: He lowered the window, and looked out at the rising sun.
en: He rolled down the window and looked out at the rising sun.

raw: There was a ridge of ploughed land, with a plough upon it where it had been left last night when the horses were unyoked; beyond, a quiet coppice-wood, in which many leaves of burning red and golden yellow still remained upon the trees.
en: There was a ridge of plowed land, with a plow sitting where it had been left the night before when the horses were unharnessed. Beyond that was a quiet woods, where many leaves of burning red and golden yellow still hung on the trees.

raw: Though the earth was cold and wet, the sky was clear, and the sun rose bright, placid, and beautiful. “Eighteen years!” said the passenger, looking at the sun. “Gracious Creator of day!
en: Although the ground was cold and wet, the sky was clear, and the sun rose bright, calm, and beautiful. "Eighteen years!" said the passenger, looking up at the sun. "Gracious Creator of the day!

raw: To be buried alive for eighteen years!”
en: To be buried alive for eighteen years!"
